name: Ensoniq Mirage
originalPurpose: A sampling keyboard at a price a working musician could actually reach, at a moment when sampling otherwise meant a Fairlight and the cost of a house.
whatActuallyHappened: It sold nearly eight thousand units in its first year, more than every other sampler on the market combined, and put recording-and-replaying sound into ordinary bedrooms. Its eight-bit sampling was noisy and its memory was tiny, neither of which turned out to matter. Derrick May built 'Strings of Life' on one, out of a piano part his friend Michael James had played at his house, sped up and cut into loops.
priceStory: 1,695 US dollars at launch, against five figures for the samplers it was competing with. The gap between those two numbers is the reason a Detroit teenager could own one.
hook: The sampler that cost as much as a used car rather than as much as a house.
blurb: Sampling means recording a sound and then playing it back at different pitches from a keyboard. Until 1984 the machines that did it cost more than a house, so only famous studios had them. The Mirage cost about as much as a used car, and it is where sampling stopped being a technique for elite studios and became an ordinary way to make music. It was noisy, eight-bit, and could only hold a couple of seconds, and it still sold more in its first year than every other sampler put together, because being able to afford it mattered more than being good. Those limits pushed users toward short loops and hard edits, and the records of the next decade can be heard being shaped by them.
